ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Land rights to tribals 
*621  SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA:†† 
SHRI C. PERUMAL: 
Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Ministry of Environment and Forests has 
rejected his Ministry's proposed Bill on providing rights to tribals in various areas; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the existing rules and guidelines on the rights 
of tribals in forests are not sufficient to meet the objective; and 
(d) if so, the areas where it is required to be improved upon? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) to (d) 
A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
††The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shrimati N.P. Durga. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [9 May, 2005] 
Statement 
(a) to (d) This Ministry was manda ted to formulate a comprehensive 
Central Legislation to redress the historical injustice done to forest dwelling tribal 
communities and for clear assertion of their legal rights on land and other 
traditional rights. This Ministry has pr epared a draft "The Scheduled Tribes 
Recognition of Forest Rights Bill, 2005", to provide a legislative frame for 
recognition of forest rights of the forest dwelling scheduled tribes, in 
consultation with the concerned Ministries, including the Ministry of 
Environment & Forests. 
The tenurial and access rights of forest dwelling Scheduled Tribes in respect 
of forest land, which they have been traditionally inhabiting for ages have not 
been adequately recognized under the existing rules and guidelines. The 
proposed Bill, therefore, seeks to recognize such rights on land, minor forest 
produce, etc. for bpnafide livelihood needs of the forest dwe lling Scheduled 
Tribes. The proposed Bill is still a tentative draft Bill and to be finalized as per the 
established procedure taking views and comments of the stakeholder Ministries, 
including Ministry of Environment & Forest into consideration 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Sir, the hon. Minister has said in his reply that he 
was still taking the views, including the Ministry of Environment and Forests. 
The Ministry of Environment and Forests has already rejected this Bill stating 
that the Tribal Affairs Ministry has no jurisdiction to legislate this Bill, since 
the distribution of forest-land is the mandate given to the Department of 
Forests. I would like to have the Minister's reaction on this. 
I would like to know from the hon. Minister why his Ministry is insisting on 
giving farming rights to tribals as well as rights over forest produce. Why can't 
the Ministry agree to give traditional rights and legally enforceable rights to 
them? 
SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the first point that I must make 
clear here is that our Ministry has been mandated to formulate a 
comprehensive Central legislation to redress the historical injustice done to the 
forest-dwelling tribal communities. There is no difference as such. Our Bill is 
still at the draft stage. It is a tenta tive draft. We are seeking the views, 
according to the laid down procedures, from all the stakeholder Ministries, 
including the Ministry of Environment and Forests. The entire meaning of 
this Bill is to see that the rights of the forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes, who 
have been living in the forest for

generations, even for centuries, are recognised. As you know very well, many 
of the tribals are dwelling in the forests. Since they do not have any rights, 
what happens is that they are treated as encroachers on many occasions, and, 
as a result of,that, there is an imperative need to have this Bill. We are 
proceeding in the right direction. 
SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Sir, my second supplementary is that the 
Ministry is emphasising on giving rights only to scheduled tribals and 
excluded non-scheduled tribal forest-dwellers from the ambit of the proposed

accommodate them, as recommended by the Technical Committee which

SHRI P.R. KYNDJAH: Sir, we are very much concerned with the other

starting with, we are beginning with, the tribals who are living in the forests 
for so long.

from the primitive tribal groups, which is about 1.4 per cent. Since he has 
opined that the existing laws are not helpful to the tribals, he has prepared the 
Bill. There is a news item, which is widely published, that the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests disagreed with the proposal. He went to the Prime 
Minister and he tried to convince him. I would like to know from the hon. 
Minister the latest status of the Bill. He says that it is only at the drafting 
stage, whereas many newspaper reports say that it is rejected, or, disagreed

MR. CHAIRMAN: You please come to your question. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: I am coming to that, Sir. 
What are the salient features of the Bill ? What are the rights that you want to 
give to the tribals, especially, to safeguard their interests? 
SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I must clarify here that there is no 
difference of opinion between the Ministry of Tribal Affairs and the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests. We are, as a matter of fact, seeking views of

all the concerned Ministries. We will reconcile whatever views are there. In fact, 
this Bill has two primary objectives. The first objective is to undo the historical 
injustice or wrong done to the Tribals. That is number one. Secondly, we are 
also very much concerned about conservation, ecological balance and environment.

ample provision for consideration. We feel that the Tribal, who is living in 
forests, is the most effective conservationist because he lives in the forest; he 
lives by the produce of the forest and he lives for the forest. Therefore, he is the best

Statement 
(a) The National Bravery Awards for children were instituted by the Indian 
Council for Child Welfare in 1957. The Indian Council for Child Welfare was 
registered as a non-government organisation under the Societies Registration 
Act XXI of 1860 on 5th June, 1952. The Awards are presented by the Hon'ble 
Prime Minister of India prior to Republic Day every year. The Awardees 
subsequently participate in the Republic Day parade. Prominent social 
workers, representatives of NGOs and re presentatives of various Government 
Departments form part of the Selection Committee. 
ICCW has taken the initiative to intr oduce a number of benefits for the 
Awardees' development and career progression with the active support and 
cooperation of the Government of India. These include the following:

(maximum of two in a year) 
(ii) The Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department of 
Education reserves seats in Diploma and Degree courses in 
Engineering (maximum three each in a year) for the Awardees. 
(iii) The Ministry of Railways provides free rail travel facilities upto 18 
years of age. 
In addition ICCW provides the following facilities for the development of the

course of study and eligibility.

Contribution of women in public life 
*637. SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the contribution of the women political elite to national life has 
been assessed by the National Commission for Women through a study by the 
Shivaji University, Kolhapur; 
(b) the recommendations of the study report on the subject of reservations for 
women in the legislature; and 
(c) Government's view on these recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) and (b) The National Commission for Women (NCW) has 
conducted a research study on the subject: 'Contribution of Women in Political 
Elite: Implications for Women's Empowerment'through the Centre for Women's 
Studies, ShivajiUniversity, Kolhapur, Maharashtra. The main recommendations 
of the study are given in the Statement. (See below) 
(c) The National Common Minimum Programme of the Government has stated 
that the Government will take the lead to introduce legislation for one-third 
reservation for women in the House of the People and the Legislative 
Assemblies of the States. 
Statement 
Recommendations relating to reservation for women contained in the 
research study on the subject: 'Contribution of Women in Political 
Elite: Implications for Women's Empowerment' commissioned by 
the National Commission for Women 
(1) Reservations per se do not guarantee effective participation of 
women. Special efforts are required for equipping women to perform 
elective roles. Political parties must gear up their machinery towards 
fresh recruitment drives and rigorous training processes for women. 
(2) Wider public debate must be initiated and encouraged in order to develop 
a clear understanding of various complex issues involved in this policy 
of reservations. 
44 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(3) It should be made obligatory on all political parties to amend their 
constitutions in order to provide for 33% reservation for women at every 
level and in every wing of party organisations. 
(4) Minimum Common Agenda for women must be chalked out. Efforts 
should be made to see that all women representatives commit 
themselves to this agenda and lobby for pushing it forwarded within their 
own party as well as in the House, across party lines. 
(5) Constituencies reserved for women must be determined not by a draw of 
lots but by a definite sequence in rotations. This will reduce uncertainty and 
also the arbitrary element and give some breathing space to the parties 
and the aspirants. 
(6) Reservation of 1/3rd seats in various committees of Municipal 
Corporations, State Legislatures and Parliament must be provided. This will 
ensure women's exposure to all the intricacies of legislative affairs. 
(7) Women's Reservation Bill must be suitably amended in order to 
remove the drawback of the provision of rotation of reservation. 
(8) Reservations at state and nationa l level need not be an eternal 
phenomenon. The policy must be reviewed after 15 years. Fifteen years is 
a sufficient period as it will cover all the constituencies at least once. 
(9) Women's quota in party organization should be introduced and should 
stretch beyond 15 years limit. This would create a large pool of 
dynamic women candidates. 
(10) There should be reservation for women in Rajya Sabha and 
Legislative Councils as well.

(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI MD. ALI ASHRAF FATMI): (a) to (d) The extent 
National Policy on Education (NPE) implies that, up to a given level, all 
students irrespective of castes, creed, location or sex have access to education 
of a comparable quality. It includes a common educational structure, a national 
curriculum framework and minimum levels of learning for each stage of 
education. 
Free and compulsory education for all children in the 6-14 year age group

legislation to enforce the Right is currently under formulation. Once enacted, this 
legislation would provide the supporting statutory mechanism for the

of uniform quality, Committees of the Central Advisory Board of Education have 
been set up on the subject of "Universalisation of Secondary Education" and 
"Girls Education and the Common School System". However, further steps on 
these issues would have to be based on wide consultations with the State 
Governments/UT Administrations, taking into account; the varying situation in 
the different States, the priorities of the various competing sectors and the availability 
of necessary resources. 
As regards higher education, the University Grants Commission, which is a 
statutory body, is responsible for the coordination, determination and 
maintenance of standards of university education. The AII India Council for 
Technical Education, which is also a statutory body, coordinates development 
of technical education, promotion of qualitative improvement in relation to 
quantitative growth and maintenance of norms and standards. The Government is 
committed to ensuring that these bodies, the universities as well as the institutions 
of higher learning and professional education provide quality education while 
retaining their autonomy.

THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) Doordarshan and All India Radio have their own Programme and 
Advertising Codes. The code inier-aiia, prohibit telecast/ broadcast of any programme or 
advertisement, which contains anythings obscene or hurts religious sentiments and offend 
religious susceptibilities. Doordarshan and All India Radio scrupulously abide by the 
codes while 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
114 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
telecasting/broadcasting their programmes. No specific complaints have been received, in

The programme of all Satellite Channels, when transmitted/retransmitted through cable 
television networks in the country, are required to adhere to the Programmes and 
Advertising Codes prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 
1995 and Rules framed there under. The Programme Code prohibits carriage of such 
programmes in Cable Service, which offend good taste or decency contain anything obscene 
or denigrates women through the depiction in any manner of the figure of a women, her 
form or body or any part there of in such a way as to have the effect of being indecent, or 
derogatory to women or is likely to deprave, corrupt or injure the public morality or morals,

unrestricted public exhibition. 
Action for violations of the codes can be taken by any authorized officer i.e. SDM, DM or 
Commissioner of Police or any other officer notified in the official gazette by the Central 
Government or State Government. 
The Central Government has constituted two inter-ministerial committee under Section 20 
of the Cable TV Networks (Regulation) Act 1995 to look into the violation of the Programme 
and Advertising Code. The Committee also takes cognizance of such violations suo-
moto. 
The Government has decided to set up a Broadcasting Regulatory Authority to 
receive and dispose of complaints on content on TV channels. A Core Group has already 
been set up in the Ministry to deliberate and draft the Bill in this regard. 
Press in India is free from Government control. The Press Council of India (PCI) is a 
statutory authority established for preserving the freedom of the Press and for maintaining and 
improving the standards of newspapers and news agencies in India. PCI has set the Norms for 
Journalists Conduct according to which Newspapers/Journalists shall not publish anything 
which is obscence, vulgar or offensive to public good taste or which has a tendency to 
malign or hurt the religious sentiments of any community or any section of society. 
The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) certifies films in accordance 
with the Cinematograph (Certification) Rules and Guidelines issued thereunder. While 
certifying films the CBFC ensures that anti-social activities, violence, sexual scenes, 
vulgarity, scenes glorifying or justifying drinking and smoking etc. are not shown. 
While certifying the

Functioning of Indian Institute of Mass Communication 
4869. SHRIMATI KUM KUM RAI: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any complaints about the functioning of the Indian Institute of Mass 
Communication have been received recently; 
(b) if so, details thereof with regard to the strength of Institute-students, the faculty and 
the names of the Board of Governors; 
(c) the revenue receipts and expenditure on various heads alongwith the budgetary 
support from his Ministry; and 
(d) governments plan for its reorganisation and economy? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPALREDDY):(a)No,Sir. 
(b) The strength of students in regular diploma Courses is 195 at Indian Institute of Mass 
Communication (IIMC), New Delhi and 55 at its branch at Dhenkanal. In addition about 500 
persons are trained through short-term courses. The sanctioned strength of faculty at IIMC, 
New Delhi is 25 and at Dhenkanal branch is 2. Name of the members of the IIMC Society 
and its Executive Council is at Statement-! • (See below) 
(c) The details are at Statement-!! (See below) 
(d) Government has decided to strengthen IIMC at Delhi and make available its 
human resources etc. to other centres on the basis of a plan proposal under the 10th Plan 
namely 'Collaboration with Regional Centres of Learning'. The rationale behind this 
scheme is to build upon the advantages of a strong local institution such as a university 
and thereby strengthen the activities of IIMC in a meaningful and locally relevant manner. 
The IIMC strictly follows the economy instructions announced from time to time by 
Government relating to such institutions.

4870. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of high-power, low-power and very low power T.V. 
Transmitters, capacity-wise, location-wise and State-wise; 
(b) whether Government have received requests from the various States for 
setting up and conversion of VLPT/LPT/HPTS during the last three years; 
and 
(c) if so, the details thereof, State-wise, and the action taken by 
Government thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Prasar Bharati has informed that 1,401 transmitters of 
varying capacity (HPTs-195, LPTs-828, VLPTs-359 and Transposers-19) are 
presently functioning in the country. State-wise details are given in the Statement 
(See below). 
(b) and (c) Requests for setting up of new transmitters as well as 
upgradation of existing transmitters are received from time to time from 
various quarters including State Governments, and these are considered while 
formulating plans of TV expansion. In the meanwhile a free to air Ku - Band 
DTH service of Doordarshan (DD Direct*) has been launched to provide 
coverage to hitherto uncovered areas. The DTH bouquet consists of 33 TV and 12 
Radio (AIR) channels. It is possible to receive DTH signals anywhere in the 
country (except A&N Islands) with the help of a small sized dish receive 
system.

Discrimination against women journalists 
4879      SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether his Ministry has gone through the Report released jointly by the 
National Commission for women and the Press Institute of India which says 
that majority of the women journalists are discriminated against by men at work 
places; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken by his Ministry to rectify the situation? . 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Main recommendations of the report are given in the Statement 
(See below). 
(c) Action on the recommendations is to be taken by various Ministries/ 
Departments including Ministry of Labour and Employment, National 
Commission for Women, Ministry of Human Resource Development, Press 
Council of India and the newspaper houses. 
Statement 
Main Recommendations of the Report 
Gender sensitisation 
* Gender sensitisation both for men and women. This can be done through 
the Press Academy in Hyderabad in collaboration with the NCW and 
PII for other parts of the country. 
* Introduction of gender writing in journalism courses with a threefold 
objective—to view language, understand issues concerned and to help 
journalists' to learn to deal with gender issues. NCW could work with 
the University Grants Commission to deal with this issue. 
* Gender-sensitisation courses especially at under-graduate level. 
154 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* There should be uniform conditions for leave, wage increase for men 
and women. 
* A difference can be made to media output by giving thought to 
gender differentiation and bringing equity to the workplace. 
Training 
* Enthusiasm often watered down by unresponsive organizations that are 
not sensitive to gender specific requirements which are often viewed 
as liabilities. 
* A male journalist is often given guidance by an experienced senior 
male colleague on entering the profession. Women journalists have no 
such apprenticeship. 
* Training and information sessions are a must to confidently operate in 
the environment and also to change mindsets. 
* Women journalists should be trained on how to negotiate contracts, 
this can be done by the NUJ/DUJ etc. so that women journalists 
know what they are entitled to. There should be transparency in policy 
matters. 
* Periodic upgradation of skills, knowledge and technology. 
* Encourage people to take sabbaticals. 
* Encourage more lateral movement and recognise contribution to 
check stagnation. 
* Regional Press should encourage women into hard reporting-politics, 
mainstream, production etc. so that promotions are easier. 
* Regular training, re-orientation. 
* Efforts to combat frustration on the desk. 
* Zero tolerance should become the norm, pushed by organizations. 
* Performance based promotions based on periodic appraisal. 
Working conditions 
* Basic facilities should be provided in offices as per requirements 
of women employees, especially toilets and canteen. 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [9 May, 2005] 
* Women should be appointed at the top level management, they might 
be able to help other women. 
* There should be some rules and regulations to maintain discipline in 
organizations. 
* Transfer should not be used to victimise women journalists. 
* Food facilities should be provided  during overtime, or night shift 
because women are unable to go out and have dinner at hotel/ dhabas 
in the night. 
* Packed dinner should be served on night shifts. 
Sexual harassment 
* NCW should run campaigns on sexual harassment. NCW could have 
an interactive session with media managements on how to identify 
sexual harassment cases. 
* A complaint box could be introduced in view of the Supreme Court 
decision on the Vishaka case. While each organization should have 
its own box, others could have a box at their respective press 
academies—where they exist. 
* Since cells have not been set up in most newspaper organizations the 
Government should re-issue the circular. 
* Newspaper organizations should report to the NCW on the 
progress of setting up these cells. 
* NCW should ask all newspaper orga nizations to report about the 
formation and constitution of the cells and list out its members. 
* Ombudsperson to look into sexual harassment cases. 
* Could a cell be set up in the Press Council to hear specifically about 
issues related to women journalists—such as their transfers, 
promotions, nightshirts, maternity leave, special needs and sexual 
harassment etc.

has asked this Ministry to tighten laws to arrest the growing trends towards 
"commodification of women and their derogatory portrayal in films, television, 
advertisement, cable or cyber network, electronic or print media etc."; 
(b) if so, whether existence of relevant laws and their ineffective en-
forcement are contributory factors towards this growing menace; and 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [9 May, 2005] 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI S. 
JAIPAL REDDY): (a) In the workshop held by NCW (National Commission for 
Women) and CBFC, concerns over content were discussed. A workshop with 
the concerned stakesholders where Chairperson CBFC was also invited, was 
also held on 16.02.05. CBFC has been of the view that content on TV need, to 
be regulated better especially music videos and adult films. 
(b) and (c) The Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) certifies films in 
accordance with the provisions under the Cinematograph Act, 1952 and the 
guidelines framed thereunder. The guidelines inter alia stipulates the following: 
* Human sensibilities are not offended by vulgarity, obscenity, or 
depravity; 
* Words with dual meaning as obviously  cater to baser instincts are not 
allowed; 
* Scenes degarding or denigrating women in any manner are not 
presented. 
Scenes showing sexual perversions shall be avoided and if such matters are 
germane to the theme, they shall be reduced to the minimum and no details are 
shown. 
As per the present position of all satellite TV channels (whether uplinked from 
India or abroad), transmitted/retransmitted through the cable network are required 
to adhere to the Programme and Adver tising Code prescribed under the Cable 
Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 and rules framed thereunder. Similarly, 
Advertising Code prescribes that advertising carried in the cable service shall 
be so designed as to conform to the laws of the country and should not offend 
morality, decency and religious susceptibilities of the subscribers. The Central 
Government has constituted an Inter-Ministerial Committee under Section 20 
of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 to look into the violations 
of the Programme and Advertising Code. The enforcement of both the 
Cinematograph Act, 1952 and the Cable Networks Regulation Act, 1995 lies 
with the State Governments. 
The Press Council of India (PCI) is a statutory, autonomous body set up 
under the Press Council Act, 1978 with twin object of preserving the

freedom of the Press and of maintaining and improving the standards of 
newspapers and news agencies in India and to inculcate principles of self-
regulation among the Press. The Government follows a policy of non-
interference in the functioning of the Council and it enjoys complete 
autonomy in its functioning. The Counc il which is the nature of a self-
regulatory body of the Press has built norms of journalistic conduct which covers 
principles and ethics with regard to journalism as also guidelines on reporting 
the specific issues of public and national importance. Further, it may also be added

  Statement-III  
The steps taken by Government for eradication of illiteracy among Scheduled 
Castes 
Education is in the Concurrent List of the Constitution and school education is 
primarily the responsibility of State Governments. The Central Government, on 
its part, supports various initiatives of the State Govern-ments. The Sarva 
Shiksha Abhiyan (SSA) and its components, District Prirary Education 
Programme (DPEP), National Programme of Nutritional Support to Primary 
Education (NPNSPE), Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalayas (KGBVs), Mahila 
Samakhya (MS), National Programme for Education of Girls at Elementary 
Level (NPEGEL), Shiksha Karmi Project (SKP) are some of the Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes for supporting the initiatives taken by the State Governments 
to provide education to children in the age group 6-14 years besides 
mainstreaming out-of-school children and dropouts. Some interventions aimed at 
bringing into the mainstream to the children from the socially weaker sections 
of society are: 
* Relaxed norms for opening of primary/Middle schools in SC 
habitations. 
* Abolition of tuition fee in all States in Government Schools at least 
upto the upper primary level. 
* Incentives like free textbooks, uniforms, stationery, school bags, 
scholarships, opening of alternative schooling facilities in unserved 
180 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
habitations, trainging of community leaders with the objectives to 
mobilize SC communities for enrolment of their children, bridge 
courses/remedial teaching, engagement of teachers from local 
communities, construction of hostels for SC boys and girls, etc. 
* SCs are given 15% reservation in Kendriya Vidyalayas (KVs) and 
Navodaya Vidyalayas (NVs). 
* Department of Elementary Educa tion and Literacy has earmarked 
notionally Rs. 900 crore for SCP out of the plan outlay of Rs. 6000 
crore for Annual Plan 2004-05. 
* The Government of India has launched National Literacy Mission to 
eradicate adult illiteracy. 
* Programmes are broadcast/telecast in Hindi and Regional Languages 
for spreading awareness ab out the various welfare 
Schemes/Literacy Programmes of the Government. Awareness is also 
spread through print media.

Tribal artisans under new WTO regime 
4911. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the traditional tribal artisans would be protected under new WTO 
regime; 
(b) whether Government are considering to unveil a new tribal welfare policy 
to address the concerns of the tribals; and 
(c) the protection being provided to ensure that tribal people would not be 
uprooted from their traditional vocations under the new trade regime? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) to (c) 
As indicated by the Ministry of Commerce, under the provisions of the TRIPS 
Agreement of WTO, protection is provided to seven categories of intellectual 
property rights, viz. copyright and related rights, patents, geographical 
indications, trademarks, industrial designs, layout-designs of integrated circuits 
and undisclosed information. In addition, protection is also provided to new 
plant varieties. Works of traditional tribal artisans are prior art and their traditional 
knowledge fall under public domain and therefore these do not belong to any of the 
above seven categories of intellectual property rights. As such, at present no 
protection is available to works of traditional tribal artisans as well as their 
traditional knowledge under the TRIPS Agreements of WTO. 
Tribal Co-operative Marketing Development Federation of India Limited 
(TRIFED) is running a tribes shop for marketing tribal arts and crafts for 
benefit of scheduled tribes artisans. 
The Department of Culture, Ministry of Tourism and Culture also implement a 
scheme of "Promotion and Dissemination of tribal/Folk Art and Culture" 
which covers the well-identified and urgent need for the preservation, promotion 
and dissemination of tribal art and culture. 
187 

RAJYA SABHA [9 May, 2005]

Ownership of tribals over MFP 
4918. SHRI NABAM REBIA: Will the Minister of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether ownership of tribals over Minor Forest Produce (MFP) is being 
given due recognition by Government; 
(b) if so, the details of Government's policy in this regard; and 
(c) the role of the Panchayats therein? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) to (c) 
Yes, Sir. The provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) 
Act, 1996 (PESA, 1996), enacted by the Government, gives the rights of 
ownership of Minor Forest Produce (MFP) to the Panchayats at the appropriate 
level and the respective Gram Sabhas. Each State Government is, therefore, 
required to amend its Panchayati Raj Act to incorporate the provisions of PESA. 
The Ministry has asked the State Governments to confer ownership rights in 
respect of minor forest produce (MFP), including tendu patta, on the Scheduled 
Tribes are providing definition of MFP, which should be all the traditional 
produce being produced by all the tribals, by amending the concerned State 
Legislations, as provided in the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the 
Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996. The Ministry of Environment & Forests has also 
drafted a Model "State Minor Forest Produce (Ownership of Forest Dependent 
Community) Bill, 2004" for conferring ownership right of MFP on local 
communities.

Statement 
Details of Revised Guidelines of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry 
Government of India 
Ministry of Commerce & Industry 
Department of Industry Policy & Promotion 
SIA (FC Division) 
Press Note 2 (2005) 
Sub.:  Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) in townships, housing, built-up 
infrastructure and construction-development projects. 
With a view to catalysing investment in townships, housing, built-up 
infrastructure and construction-development projects as an instrument to generate 
economic activity, create new employment opportunities and add to the 
available housing stock and built-up infrastructure, the Government has 
decided to allow FDI up to 100% under the automatic route in townships, 
housing, built-up infrastructure and construction-development projects (which 
would include, but not be restricted to, housing, commercial premises, hotels, 
resorts, hospitals, educational instituti ons, recreational facilities, city and 
regional level infrastructure), subject to the following guidelines; 
(a) Minimum area to be developed under each project would be as under: 
218 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(i) In case of development of serviced housing plots, a minimum land 
area of hectares. 
(ii) In case of construction-development projects, a minimum built-up 
area of 50,000 sq. mts. 
(iii) In case of a combination pr oject, any one of the above two 
conditions would suffice. 
(b) the investment would further be subject to the following conditions: 
(i) Minimum capitalization of US $ 10 million for wholly owned 
subsidiaries and US $ 5 million for joint ventures with Indian 
partners. The funds would have to be brought in within six months of 
commencement of business of the Company. 
(ii) Original investment cannot be repatriate before a period of three years 
from completion of minimum capitalization. However, the investor 
may be permitted to exit earlier with prior approval of the 
Government through the FIPB. 
(c) At least 50 of the project must be developed within a period of five years 
from the date of obtaining all statutory clearances. The investor would not be 
permitted to sell undeveloped plots. For the purpose of these guidelines, 
"undeveloped plots" will mean where roads, water supply, street lighting, drainage, 
sewerage, and other conveni ences, as applicable under prescribed regulations, 
have not been made available. It will be necessary that the investor provides this 
infrastructure and obtains the completion certificate from the concerned local 
body/service agency before he would be allowed to dispose of serviced housing 
plots. 
(d) The project shall conform to the norms and standards, including land 
use requirements and provision of community amenities and common facilities, 
as laid down in the applicable building control regulations, bye-laws, rules, and 
other regulations of the States Government/Municipal/Local Body concerned. 
(e) The investor shall be responsible for obtaining all necessary approvals, 
including those of the building/layout plans, developing internal and peripheral 
areas and other infrastructure facilities, payment of development, external 
development and other charges and complying with all other requirements as 
prescribed under applicable rules/bye-laws/regulations of the State 
Govemment/Municipal/Local Body concerned. 
219

(f) The State Government/Municipal/Local Body concerned, which approves 
the building/development plans, would monitor compliance of the above 
conditions by the developer.

Revision of poverty alleviation targets 
4945. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA : Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have revised the target set for the Tenth Five Year 
Plan regarding alleviation of poverty prevailing in the cities; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps taken to achieve the target set under such programme 
alongwith the success achieved in relation thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN EMPLOY-
MENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) to (c) The • 
Tenth Five Year Plan period (2002—2007) has set a target for reduction of poverty 
by 5 percentage points by the year 2007 and by 15 percentage points by 2012. 
The Tenth Plan does not specify any separate targets for reducing poverty levels 
in cities. 
In the urban areas, Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation is 
implementing an employment oriented Urban Poverty Alleviation Programme 
named Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), on all India basis, 
through States/Union Territories, with effect from 01.12.1997. The scheme 
envisages to provide gainful employment to the urban unemployed and 
underemployed poor .through, firstly, encouraging the setting up of self-
employment ventures by those who have studied upto 9th standard and, secondly, 
by providing wage employment by utilizing their labour for construction of 
socially and economically useful public assets. 
220 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
During the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002—07), on all India basis, targets to 
provide 4,00,000 employment opportunities to the urban poor, through setting up 
of micro/group enterprises and to impart skill training to 5,00,000 persons have 
been fixed under SJSRY. During the first three years of the Tenth Plan, i.e. from 
2002-2003 to 2004-2005, comulatively, 2,97,419 micro-enterprises have been set up 
and 3,27,399 urban poor have been provided skill training.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
Situation arising out of the large scale devastation caused by 
Tsunami on 26th December, 2004. 
SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN (Kerala): Sir, in this august House, we are 
discussing an unexpected human tr agedy, which occurred on 26th 
December. At the outset, I would pay homage to thousands of victims who lost 
their lives in this unexpected tragedy. 
Sir, tsunami is a new kind of natural calamity, which we never faced before in 
our country. I have had the opportunity to visit some of the tsunami-affected areas. Of 
course, not only me, right from the Prime Minister to a good number of Union 
Cabinet Ministers, social activists, State Ministers and MPs had also visited and 
extended all kinds of support to victims of this tragedy. While we are discussing 
this tsunami issue, there are two things that we have to discuss seriously. 
One issue is the failure in assessing the situation and to provide sufficient 
warnings, which would have been more helpful to extend rescue work. Sir, it 
was reported that when tsunami tidal waves started in the eastern part of Asia, 
the U.S. Tsunami Warning Centre at Los Angeles had detected the arrival of tsunami, 
248 

[9 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
but it did not know whom to inform about it in India. It means that we do 
not have a system to assess this kind of seismic problems. So, this is the 
important issue, which we have to discuss. 
Wny did it happen? We have developed science and technology; we 
have developed atmosphere and ocean sciences; and our country also 
claims that we have the third largest number of scientific community in the 
world. Only day before yesterday, we complimented our scientific 
community in this House. Till now, we do not know why we failed to given 
sufficient warning to the people. This was an international tragedy. In our 
country, it occurred first in the Andamans, then after six hours, it came to 
Tamil Nadu, and then another two hours later, it came to Kerala. We were 
not in a position to provide sufficient warnings to our poor people who were 
staying in coastal areas. Had we been able to given sufficient warning, we 
would have been in a position to evacuate larger number of population. 
This is an experience, which we gained. At a later date when we got the 
information about tsunami again from the Central Government, the Ministry 
of Science and Technology, people were evacuated. Nothing happened 
because now a system was there. It wa s all due to the initiative of the 
Government. Once a tragedy occurred, then from that experience, we can 
give warning and do rescue work in future. That is possible. Why I am 
discussing this matter here in this House, because we have a failure in 
this country not only in the case of tsunami but also in all kinds of natural 
calamities that have occurred, whether tornado or any such incident. We 
do not have a system to protect our people. If such kind of natural calamity 
as this takes place in the Western countries, they are able to evacuate 
their people. They will be able to save the lives of the common men. In 
India,'so far, we do not have any such devices to protect or evacuate our 
general public from the natural calamities even though we do get sufficient 
information in advance. So, from the experience of tsunami, what the 
Government is going to do with regard to developing a system in our country 
to evacuate the people and save their lives from natural calamities?

ered by the Cabinet. Then, it was referred to the Ministers' Committee.

SHRI TARIQ ANWAR (Maharashtra): Sir, it needs no repetition that the 
agricultural sector holds an important place in the Indian economy. The 
productivity of Indian agriculture is very poor. India ranks at or near bottom

varieties originally imported from India. In rice, Indian yields are one-third

the level achieved in South Africa. Prductivity in pulses is one-tenth the 
level of France. In groundnut, Indian yields are one-sixth Israel's average.

the USA. Israel's food and agricultural output valued at 4 billion US dollars, 
is produced on just one million acres of very arid land. India has 400 
million acres of land at its disposal. Imagine what we can achieve with 
such productivity!

of analysing the soil for all its 13 nutrients. Such a programme would also 
have to be accompanied by a training programme of district and block 
level agriculture functionaries who would have the responsibility to develop 
new techniques for growing various crops, based on the results of soil 
tests, and make suitable recommendations to the farmers.

SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, my 
Special Mention relates to the need to take urgent measures for 
stopping SIM card cloning. Recent detection of rampant cloning of 
Global System for Mobile Communication, SIM has raised serious 
questions over matters of security, not only of mobile users but also of 
the country, in view of suspected use of such technology for 
organised crime and other unscrupulous activities. Cases of SIM Card 
cloning are going up. The 
285 

RAJYA SABHA [9 May, 2005] 
problem is, fast developments in the world of communications have made 
certain equipments available in the market, which are being abused by 
miscreants. The miscreants are obtaining gadgets which are easily available 
in the market like SIM readers and software, which can be used to extract 
feed details of one card to another. Technology used to clone these SIM 
Cards is similar to the one used by criminals to clone credit cards by 
using skimmers. Similarly, to create copies of GSM Cards, culprits use 
SIM reader to download its data Then, computer software is used to 
decrypt data to retrieve Integrated Circuit Card Identification (ICCID), 
International Mobile Security Identification (IMSI), Short Messaging Service 
Identification (SMSI) and authentication key numbers, apart from personal 
data. The software then used to transpose vital information on another 
card, after that it will become identical to the original ones. Users of such 
cards cannot be tracked down easily. Apart from individual financial loss, 
such cards provide opportunity to criminals to remain in touch with each 
other without fear of being racked down easily. So, there is very likelihood 
of this modus operandi being employed by anti-national elements to achieve 
their goals without being deteced. Hence, I request the Government of 
India to immediately take measures to stop SIM cloning in the national 
interest. Thank you.

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): Sir, I move:—
